Theme

Conversation, family & daily routines

wake up verb

also wake, awaken, waken, arouse from sleep, wake someone up

classical

Plin. Ep. 9.36.1: ēvigilō cum libuit
Traupman 403

ēvigilō, ēvigilāre, ēvigilāvī, ēvigilātum

verb, first conjugation

Pliny’s and Quintilian’s verb in this sense (Lewis & Short).

Other words

  • expergīscor, expergīscī, experrēctus sum

    verb, third conjugation, deponent · also used · classical · Cic. Att. 2.23.3: sī dormīs expergīscere; Liv. 1.39.2: dōnec suā sponte experrēctus esset; Traupman 39, 403: wake up, intr.

    Cicero’s and Livy’s verb.

  • (ē somnō) excitāre — wake someone up

    excitō, excitāre, excitāvī, excitātum, transitive · also used · classical · Cic. Rep. 6.12: quaesō, nē mē ē somnō excitētis (Lewis & Short s.v. excitō); Traupman 403

    Transitive: you wake someone else with excitāre; you wake up yourself with expergīscī or ēvigilāre.

Examples

  • ēvigilō cum libuit, plērumque circā hōram prīmam, saepe ante, tardius rārō

    I wake up when I like, usually about the first hour, often before, seldom laterPlin. Ep. 9.36.1

  • sī dormīs expergīscere, sī stās ingredere, sī ingrederis curre, sī curris advolā

    if you’re asleep, wake up; if you’re standing, walk; if you’re walking, run; if you’re running, flyCic. Att. 2.23.3

  • cum somnō repetītō simul cum sōle experrēctus essem

    when I had gone back to sleep and woken with the sunCic. Att. 13.38.1

  • movērī vetuisse puerum dōnec suā sponte experrēctus esset

    she forbade anyone to move the boy until he woke up of his own accordLiv. 1.39.2

  • ē somnō excitāre

    to wake someone from sleepTraupman 273

See also wake someone up, get up.
